nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name: Cynoscion arenarlus
Common Name: Sand Seatrout

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthyes
      Order: Perciformes
      Family: Sciaenidae

Other Common Names: White trout (47 265 327 691 1362); sand trout (327 581 1362); sand weakfish (581); sand squeteague (1362).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Caught mainly with bottom trawls and gillnets (791). Florida landings for
1989 totaled 56,792 lbs worth $16,974 dockside ($0.30 per lb), with all but 228 lbs landed at Florida west coast ports (902). Considered a "highly esteemed" food fish, most are marketed fresh (791). Among the most common species caught in the industrial bottom fishery of the northern Gulf of Mexico, they are primarily utilized to produce pet food (691) Important as bycatch in shrimp trawls.
Recreational:   A popular fish with most anglers throughout its range (327). Total recreational catch for the Gulf of Mexico was 2,732,000 fish in 1988 (513), and was estimated at 3,394,000 fish weighing 1,796,104 lbs in 1991 (1363). The total recreational catch for Florida in 1991 was estimated at 1,696,000 fish weighing 898,880 lbs (1363)

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Limited to the Gulf of Mexico (788 1362), from southwest Florida (603) to the Bay of Campeche (1361).
Within Study Area: Common in estuaries and bays of the west coast of Florida (691 891
1373). Most abundant in Everglades National Park in fall and winter, though never very abundant, and much more common in the northern Gulf (1373). Colby et al (1054) reported sand seatrout as the tenth most abundant fish species collected, and most abundant during July, in the bay system between Goodland and Chokoloskee.  Also reported as among the dominant species in the Ten Thousand Islands area by Carter et al (1443). Only two specimens collected (both near the Gulf) during two years of gill net sampling in Florida Bay (852 1432).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs are probably pelagic; larvae are pelagic (1283). Juveniles and adults are estuarine and demersal (47). Schools, often forming groups with Cynoscion nebulosus. Activity patterns tend to be diurnal (741).
Movements and Migrations:
Decreasing temperatures in the fall cause fish spawned late in the summer and adults to migrate from bays and estuaries to inshore Gulf waters to overwinter (255 374 553 649 664 741 751 789), but some fish remain in the estuaries throughout the winter (265 664 789). Some authors consider this a spawning migration. In Everglades National Park, however, C. arenarius were collected in the estuaries only during the fall and winter months (603). Adults move back into estuaries after spawning in the spring and summer (47). Larvae spawned in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico appear to be carried inshore from spawning grounds by longshore currents (150 649).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Marine to estuarine. Larvae have been collected in inshore to midshelf waters in depths ranging from 5 to 70 m with most larvae occurring inside the 18 m isobath (149 150). Schlossman and Chittenden (649) reported that spring and late summer spawned larvae use estuarine and inshore Gulf nurseries, but found that estuaries are the most important areas for late summer fish. It has been reported that larvae appear to have some surface orientation (149 150), but Robison (1342) found that C. arenarius dominated bottom collections at the mouth of Tampa Bay, regardless of tidal stage. Adults and juveniles prefer nearshore and inshore areas and are rarely taken in waters deeper than 55 m (255 374 470 1342). Adults have been caught offshore as deep as 110 m. Adults concentrate around oyster reefs, wrecks, and bridges preferably at depths greater than 1 m (47 226).
Substrate: The young prefer muddy bottoms (327). Larvae and juveniles prefer grass beds and marsh areas, with soft organic bottoms (131 47). Adults are found over most bottom types in estuaries and offshore (691) including oyster reefs (226).  Reported to prefer mud bottoms in the bays along the southwestern tip of Florida (1054).

nodes.title: Physical/chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: Most larvae and juveniles are taken above 10 C, however they have been reported from 5.0-35.0 C (116 136 150). Larvae mostly occur from 14.0 to 21.0 C (149) Copeland and Bechtel (136) reported optimum catches in temperatures of 20-30 C. Some have been caught in temperatures as high as 40.0 C (226). Adults prefer temperatures of 12.0-36.0 C (47 226 255 470 741). In Florida, collected at temperatures ranging from 10.0 to 33.0 C at Cedar Key (378 581), 21.1 to 31.5 C in Tampa Bay (664), 15.0 to 37.0 C in Charlotte Harbor (789), and 19.5 to 26.0 C in Everglades National Park (603). Springer and Woodburn (664) found 3 cold-killed fish in the Tampa Bay area when water temperatures were 13 C, but they also collected live specimens from Pensacola Bay at a temperature of 10.2 C.
Salinity: Larvae collected in one study were found in waters of 15-36 ppt salinity (149 150). Small sand seatrout have been reported in salinities from 0-28 ppt (116 751). Best catches for 20-90 mm TL were reported in salinities <15 ppt; fish of 90-220 mm TL were caught in salinities greater than 15 ppt (1352). Adult sand Seatrout have been caught in salinities as high as 45 ppt (651). Collected in salinities of 17.5-26.7 ppt at Cedar Key (378 581), 3.7-29.8 ppt in Tampa Bay (664), 0.09-23.0 ppt in the Caloosahatchee River estuary (265), 0.0-34.5 ppt in Charlotte Harbor (789), and 16.4-35.7 ppt in Everglades National Park (603).
Dissolved Oxygen: Sand seatrout avoid water with less than 4.6-5.0 mg/1 (47).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode: Dieocious with external fertilization.

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
Fish appear to spawn at variable depths from 7-91 m and from lower estuaries to offshore Gulf waters up to ca. 175 km from shore (150 553 648). Schlossman (1980) suggested spawning in 14-40 m depths. Most spawning appears to occur in the shallow Gulf primarily in waters between 7 to 15 m in depth (149). Sand seatrout spawn from March through September (223 226 255 483 649 664 751 1428) and possibly as early as January (649 150). Perry (553) suggested that sand seatrout spawn throughout the winter in deep water. This was based on the presence of females with roe leaking from the anal pore caught at stations in 40-50 fathoms during February and March.
Reproductive Capacity:  Sheridan et al. (648) estimated a mean fecundity of 100,990, with a range from 28,200 to 423,100 for females of 210 mm SL (142.8 gm) and 247 mm SL (365.9 gm), respectively. They (648) provided the following relationship between fecundity, standard length (mm), and ovary weight (gm):

[eq]
F -198,665 + l, 480(SL), r^2 =0.36
F -8,917 + 759(W), r^2 =0.51
F 32,539 + 7,893(OW), r^2 =0.53
[/eq]

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Juvenile: Estimated growth rate is 5.8 mm/wk (758). In Texas, fish spawned in the spring reach 160-190 mm TL after six months, and 220-280 after one year. Those spawned in late summer range from 120-150 mm TL after 6 months, and 210-250 mm TL after one year (649).  Perret and Caillouet (548) reported similar sizes for Age I fish in Louisiana.
Adult: Maturation occurs around 129 mm SL and 140 mm SL for males and females, respectively (648). Gunter (255) reported a mature male of 127 mm, also in Texas. Sex-ratio varies geographically, but is close to 1:1 (648). Sheridan et al (648) presented the following length-weight relationship:
[eq]
Log W = 4.46 + 2.86(Log SL), r^2 =.99
[/eq]
Maximum life span is estimated to be 3 years, with a maximum length of 590 mm TL (732).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Trophic Modes: Generalized predator; feeds more in daylight hours on live and dead organisms (741). Mysids and calanoid copepods are the main diet of sand seatrout less than 40 mm SL (645 647). Fish are the predominant food item of all larger sand seatrout, with the bay anchovy being the most frequently consumed prey (163 483 532 581 584 645 648 664)

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: The possible existence of ecological differences between life stages was suggested by Springer and Woodburn (664) because of the occurrence of juveniles in the bays, but with adults found primarily offshore.

Title: Sand Seatrout (Cynoscion arenarius).

FLELMR Code #: 1719

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
6/30/93. TD Phillips

Note: FL Bay data added 2/94

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Scientific Name: Cynoscion arenarlus
Common Name: Sand Seatrout

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthyes
      Order: Perciformes
      Family: Sciaenidae

Other Common Names: White trout (47 265 327 691 1362); sand trout (327 581 1362); sand weakfish (581); sand squeteague (1362).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Caught mainly with bottom trawls and gillnets (791). Florida landings for
1989 totaled 56,792 lbs worth $16,974 dockside ($0.30 per lb), with all but 228 lbs landed at Florida west coast ports (902). Considered a "highly esteemed" food fish, most are marketed fresh (791). Among the most common species caught in the industrial bottom fishery of the northern Gulf of Mexico, they are primarily utilized to produce pet food (691) Important as bycatch in shrimp trawls.
Recreational:   A popular fish with most anglers throughout its range (327). Total recreational catch for the Gulf of Mexico was 2,732,000 fish in 1988 (513), and was estimated at 3,394,000 fish weighing 1,796,104 lbs in 1991 (1363). The total recreational catch for Florida in 1991 was estimated at 1,696,000 fish weighing 898,880 lbs (1363)

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Limited to the Gulf of Mexico (788 1362), from southwest Florida (603) to the Bay of Campeche (1361).
Within Study Area: Common in estuaries and bays of the west coast of Florida (691 891
1373). Most abundant in Everglades National Park in fall and winter, though never very abundant, and much more common in the northern Gulf (1373). Colby et al (1054) reported sand seatrout as the tenth most abundant fish species collected, and most abundant during July, in the bay system between Goodland and Chokoloskee.  Also reported as among the dominant species in the Ten Thousand Islands area by Carter et al (1443). Only two specimens collected (both near the Gulf) during two years of gill net sampling in Florida Bay (852 1432).

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Eggs are probably pelagic; larvae are pelagic (1283). Juveniles and adults are estuarine and demersal (47). Schools, often forming groups with Cynoscion nebulosus. Activity patterns tend to be diurnal (741).
Movements and Migrations:
Decreasing temperatures in the fall cause fish spawned late in the summer and adults to migrate from bays and estuaries to inshore Gulf waters to overwinter (255 374 553 649 664 741 751 789), but some fish remain in the estuaries throughout the winter (265 664 789). Some authors consider this a spawning migration. In Everglades National Park, however, C. arenarius were collected in the estuaries only during the fall and winter months (603). Adults move back into estuaries after spawning in the spring and summer (47). Larvae spawned in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico appear to be carried inshore from spawning grounds by longshore currents (150 649).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type: Marine to estuarine. Larvae have been collected in inshore to midshelf waters in depths ranging from 5 to 70 m with most larvae occurring inside the 18 m isobath (149 150). Schlossman and Chittenden (649) reported that spring and late summer spawned larvae use estuarine and inshore Gulf nurseries, but found that estuaries are the most important areas for late summer fish. It has been reported that larvae appear to have some surface orientation (149 150), but Robison (1342) found that C. arenarius dominated bottom collections at the mouth of Tampa Bay, regardless of tidal stage. Adults and juveniles prefer nearshore and inshore areas and are rarely taken in waters deeper than 55 m (255 374 470 1342). Adults have been caught offshore as deep as 110 m. Adults concentrate around oyster reefs, wrecks, and bridges preferably at depths greater than 1 m (47 226).
Substrate: The young prefer muddy bottoms (327). Larvae and juveniles prefer grass beds and marsh areas, with soft organic bottoms (131 47). Adults are found over most bottom types in estuaries and offshore (691) including oyster reefs (226).  Reported to prefer mud bottoms in the bays along the southwestern tip of Florida (1054).

sections.heading: Physical/chemical
sections.content:
Temperature: Most larvae and juveniles are taken above 10 C, however they have been reported from 5.0-35.0 C (116 136 150). Larvae mostly occur from 14.0 to 21.0 C (149) Copeland and Bechtel (136) reported optimum catches in temperatures of 20-30 C. Some have been caught in temperatures as high as 40.0 C (226). Adults prefer temperatures of 12.0-36.0 C (47 226 255 470 741). In Florida, collected at temperatures ranging from 10.0 to 33.0 C at Cedar Key (378 581), 21.1 to 31.5 C in Tampa Bay (664), 15.0 to 37.0 C in Charlotte Harbor (789), and 19.5 to 26.0 C in Everglades National Park (603). Springer and Woodburn (664) found 3 cold-killed fish in the Tampa Bay area when water temperatures were 13 C, but they also collected live specimens from Pensacola Bay at a temperature of 10.2 C.
Salinity: Larvae collected in one study were found in waters of 15-36 ppt salinity (149 150). Small sand seatrout have been reported in salinities from 0-28 ppt (116 751). Best catches for 20-90 mm TL were reported in salinities <15 ppt; fish of 90-220 mm TL were caught in salinities greater than 15 ppt (1352). Adult sand Seatrout have been caught in salinities as high as 45 ppt (651). Collected in salinities of 17.5-26.7 ppt at Cedar Key (378 581), 3.7-29.8 ppt in Tampa Bay (664), 0.09-23.0 ppt in the Caloosahatchee River estuary (265), 0.0-34.5 ppt in Charlotte Harbor (789), and 16.4-35.7 ppt in Everglades National Park (603).
Dissolved Oxygen: Sand seatrout avoid water with less than 4.6-5.0 mg/1 (47).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content: Reproductive Mode: Dieocious with external fertilization.

sections.heading: Mating/Spawning
sections.content:
Fish appear to spawn at variable depths from 7-91 m and from lower estuaries to offshore Gulf waters up to ca. 175 km from shore (150 553 648). Schlossman (1980) suggested spawning in 14-40 m depths. Most spawning appears to occur in the shallow Gulf primarily in waters between 7 to 15 m in depth (149). Sand seatrout spawn from March through September (223 226 255 483 649 664 751 1428) and possibly as early as January (649 150). Perry (553) suggested that sand seatrout spawn throughout the winter in deep water. This was based on the presence of females with roe leaking from the anal pore caught at stations in 40-50 fathoms during February and March.
Reproductive Capacity:  Sheridan et al. (648) estimated a mean fecundity of 100,990, with a range from 28,200 to 423,100 for females of 210 mm SL (142.8 gm) and 247 mm SL (365.9 gm), respectively. They (648) provided the following relationship between fecundity, standard length (mm), and ovary weight (gm):

[eq]
F -198,665 + l, 480(SL), r^2 =0.36
F -8,917 + 759(W), r^2 =0.51
F 32,539 + 7,893(OW), r^2 =0.53
[/eq]

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Juvenile: Estimated growth rate is 5.8 mm/wk (758). In Texas, fish spawned in the spring reach 160-190 mm TL after six months, and 220-280 after one year. Those spawned in late summer range from 120-150 mm TL after 6 months, and 210-250 mm TL after one year (649).  Perret and Caillouet (548) reported similar sizes for Age I fish in Louisiana.
Adult: Maturation occurs around 129 mm SL and 140 mm SL for males and females, respectively (648). Gunter (255) reported a mature male of 127 mm, also in Texas. Sex-ratio varies geographically, but is close to 1:1 (648). Sheridan et al (648) presented the following length-weight relationship:
[eq]
Log W = 4.46 + 2.86(Log SL), r^2 =.99
[/eq]
Maximum life span is estimated to be 3 years, with a maximum length of 590 mm TL (732).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Trophic Modes: Generalized predator; feeds more in daylight hours on live and dead organisms (741). Mysids and calanoid copepods are the main diet of sand seatrout less than 40 mm SL (645 647). Fish are the predominant food item of all larger sand seatrout, with the bay anchovy being the most frequently consumed prey (163 483 532 581 584 645 648 664)

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: The possible existence of ecological differences between life stages was suggested by Springer and Woodburn (664) because of the occurrence of juveniles in the bays, but with adults found primarily offshore.
